title: Every file in OwnBase, and how they connect
intro: OwnBase is a team chat app that you run yourself, a bit like a private Slack. People open it in a web browser or in the desktop app, and one computer runs the server that keeps the team's messages and files. On the map below, each dot is one file of code and each line is one part of OwnBase relying on another.

areas.title: What you see and click
areas.summary: Every conversation, dialog and setting on screen. The web version and the desktop app show the same screens, and each click becomes a request to the app engine.

areas.title: Keeping the app in sync
areas.summary: Keeps the app's copy of the workspace up to date, holds messages waiting to send, handles attachments and runs calls. Your work stays safe when the connection drops.

areas.title: The rules both sides follow
areas.summary: What a message, a channel, a permission, a search or a call looks like. The app and the server both follow these rules, so they always understand each other.

areas.title: Keeping the workspace
areas.summary: Checks every request, saves messages and files, and tells everyone's app what changed. It also handles accounts, connected apps, removing old messages and restoring backups.

areas.title: The app on your computer
areas.summary: Saves your data on your computer, can host a workspace for other people, makes backups, recovers when a window crashes and saves your work before it closes.

areas.title: Opening OwnBase in a browser
areas.summary: Packs the screens so they open in any web browser. The server sends them compressed, and each browser remembers its own sign-ins.

areas.title: Running the server on its own
areas.summary: The same server without the desktop app, for a home server or a rented one. A ready-made package sets it up on a server.

areas.title: The Enterprise edition
areas.summary: Features for larger organisations, source-available under their own license and switched on by a license key the server checks itself. Without a key the server is the free edition, and chat never depends on one.

areas.title: Building and checking
areas.summary: Scripts that build OwnBase, check each build matches its code, run the tests, measure speed and stop a release when something is wrong.

areas.title: Guides for hosts
areas.summary: How to host OwnBase and keep backups, how the automatic checks run, and how other apps can connect to a workspace.

areas.title: Project settings
areas.summary: The outside code OwnBase uses, settings every package shares, how to contribute and the commands that run the whole project.

areas.title: This atlas
areas.summary: The written explanations and the script that turns the project's files into this one page. The page leaves itself out of its own list.

principles.title: The server has the final say
principles.text: The app shows your change right away, but the server decides what is saved. If the server says no, the app puts things back the way the server has them.

principles.title: Unsent work always has an owner
principles.text: A draft or a message waiting to send belongs to one account and one conversation. The app remembers what was sent or thrown away, so an old window cannot lose your work or bring back a message you deleted.

principles.title: Answers can arrive late
principles.text: A reply from the server can come back after you closed the dialog, changed microphone or the host changed. Before using an answer, the code checks it still belongs to what you are doing now.

principles.title: Speed claims need numbers
principles.text: Each speed-up goes after a cost that someone measured. Read how and where it was measured before treating an old number as true today.

reading.title: Start with the map
reading.text: Click an architecture block to open its entry file. Follow the dependencies to see which layer performs each operation.

reading.title: Follow a real journey
reading.text: How it works explains an operation step by step, with the files responsible for each handoff.

reading.title: Inspect the implementation
reading.text: File explorer has reviewed runtime summaries, complete text source, declarations with line links, named tests, imports and reverse references. Press / to search file paths; enable source search to find code.

reading.title: Check a claim
reading.text: Improvements distinguishes implemented controls, historical measured changes and open follow-ups. Evidence links open the embedded original report or raw results.

limits.text: This is a snapshot of the code at one moment, not a live view. Rebuild it after the code changes.
limits.detail: This is a source snapshot, not a live monitor. Its input digest identifies the embedded files; regenerate it after changes. The base commit identifies the checkout, not a claim that all local files were committed there.

limits.text: It covers every file in the project except this page itself. Downloaded outside code, build output and personal data are left out.
limits.detail: Every tracked file is indexed except this generated HTML itself. Explicit atlas source files are added before their first commit. Ignored builds, node_modules, user data and unrelated untracked directories are not scanned.

limits.text: Every file of app code has a written explanation that a person checked. Other files, like tests and settings, get a description made from their contents.
limits.detail: All runtime source files in apps and packages have reviewed file explanations. Test, documentation, configuration and asset descriptions also use structural metadata. Generated symbol and import indexes do not infer every line's intent.

limits.text: A line between two files means one names the other in its code. It shows what depends on what, not every step the code takes while it runs.
limits.detail: Imports are static source references, including literal dynamic imports and workspace package entries. They are not a runtime call graph; type-only imports, indirect exports and injected adapters can change how the code runs.

limits.text: You can read every text file in full. Images and other files that are not text show only their size.
limits.detail: Text source is complete and paged for responsive reading. Binary assets show metadata. Symbol indexing covers named declarations, class methods and top-level values, not every anonymous closure or generated declaration.

limits.text: A speed number belongs to the computer, the version and the test it came from. A smaller download does not by itself mean the app starts faster.
limits.detail: Benchmarks belong to their recorded revision, hardware, sample count and fixture. A smaller archive does not establish faster startup. Bundle-entry limits do not measure the full import closure or decoded media memory.

limits.text: The N records are finished repairs. The Q records are problems that were found and reproduced, and each says whether it is fixed yet. Fixing one part does not fix every part that relies on it.
limits.detail: N01–N12 are completed scoped repairs. Q01–Q13 are reproduced findings; each record's status says whether it is implemented or still a follow-up. A repaired storage backend does not automatically fix its callers' preference races; bounded controller cleanup does not establish every adapter owns a partially started server.

limits.text: Some things were never tried for real: installing and removing the app, unplugging a microphone, a power cut, signing out of the computer, and reaching a workspace from another device over the internet. Deleting old messages does not remove them from older backups.
limits.detail: Recorded validation excludes genuine installed upgrade/uninstall, physical microphone unplug, power loss or OS logoff, and second-device/public routing. Active database cleanup does not erase old backups or freed disk bytes.

glossary.meaning: The app's copy of the workspace on your device. The server sends updates to keep it current.
Messages waiting to send. The app remembers which were sent or thrown away, so an old window cannot send one twice or bring it back.
Telling everyone's app, and any connected apps, about a change the server already saved. If telling them fails, the change is still saved.
A label on each request, so the app knows which answer belongs to the latest one. Two identical requests still get different labels.
Limits on how much work the app or the server takes on at once. When it is full it says no, and you can try again.
Full-text search, the way the server finds words inside messages quickly.
Rules a host sets for deleting old messages and files, including every copy and saved preview of them.
How a desktop app window asks the rest of the app to do something only the app may do, like saving a file. The app checks who is asking.
Two ways to describe a time. p50 is the typical time, and half the tries were faster. p95 is a slow case, and 95 tries in 100 were faster.
A fingerprint of the code stamped into each build, so a check can spot a build made from old or changed code.
